\begin{abstract}
As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
From each passage we extract a compact statistical fingerprint---19 candidate features dominated by perplexity tail statistics, with the top 5 achieving 97.6\% of full-set performance---computed against a fixed reference model (Pythia-1.4B).
A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%; 58.8--82.6\% when excluding the near-perfectly separable d0 class; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied $3 \times 3$ grid (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 8/9 cells, respectively).
Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%; temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a correctable scale component and a residual structural component.
Notably, cross-model recursive chains---where each depth is generated by a different architecture---achieve 84.75\% accuracy, demonstrating that the depth signal is a property of the recursive process itself rather than of any individual generator.
Extending to two 7B-scale generators yields 70.2\% accuracy with monotonic AUC decay ($\mathrm{EDD}{=}4$), while a second 7B architecture exhibits $\mathrm{EDD}{>}5$ with a non-monotonic trajectory possibly linked to instruction-tuning effects.
Applied to WikiText-103 (546 passages), all three model-specific classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy despite $+$621\% domain shift in mean perplexity; on C4 web-crawl text, false positive rates range from 4.7\% to 22.4\%, concentrated in template content.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ across models; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
5	The dominant pair (\texttt{p90\_ppl} top-2 in 9/9 cells, \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 under SHAP) generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature} within this experimental scope.
6	Recent work corroborates this connection, identifying entropy decline as a measurable signal of recursive degradation that parallels the tail erosion our features capture~\cite{shi2025_closer_look}.
7	Zero-shot LLM baselines reinforce this view: DeepSeek V3.2 (36.2\%) and Qwen2.5-7B (30.4\%) exhibit complementary failure modes---the former predicts nearly all samples as d0 while the latter is biased toward d1---yet both perform near chance, confirming that depth discrimination requires the targeted statistical features our pipeline extracts rather than general language understanding.
8	
9	Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1\% vs.\ 66.4\% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown decoding strategies infeasible.
10	A multi-temperature ablation ($\tau \in [0.5, 1.1]$, Pythia-1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:multi_tau}) reinforces this: within-$\tau$ depth discrimination is robust for $\tau \leq 0.9$ (d1v2 AUC $>0.80$), but cross-$\tau$ transfer (mean 46.7\%) is harder than cross-strategy transfer (59.1\%), confirming that strategy-conditioned classifiers are necessary.
11	A two-stage pipeline---first identifying the decoding strategy, then applying a strategy-conditioned depth classifier---could address this.
12	Different strategies produce distinguishable perplexity signatures (top-$k$ yields narrower distributions; temperature sampling produces heavier tails), suggesting that automatic strategy identification is technically feasible, though independent validation on held-out strategy sets is needed.
13	As an alternative, when deployment is restricted to a single platform or API provider, the decoding strategy is typically known a priori, and a strategy-conditioned classifier can be applied directly.
14	
15	\paragraph{Depth-graduated data curation.}
16	Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction~\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
17	Depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) while filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
18	A proof-of-concept LoRA fine-tuning experiment shows RF depth-based filtering matches unfiltered performance with 44\% of the data, significantly outperforming size-matched random subsampling at all stringency tiers (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}).
19	Cross-strategy deployment would first require strategy identification to avoid boundary inversion (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}).
20	
21	\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ across models; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
The dominant pair (\texttt{p90\_ppl} top-2 in 9/9 cells, \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 under SHAP) generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature} within this experimental scope.
Recent work corroborates this connection, identifying entropy decline as a measurable signal of recursive degradation that parallels the tail erosion our features capture~\cite{shi2025_closer_look}.
Zero-shot LLM baselines reinforce this view: DeepSeek V3.2 (36.2\%) and Qwen2.5-7B (30.4\%) exhibit complementary failure modes---the former predicts nearly all samples as d0 while the latter is biased toward d1---yet both perform near chance, confirming that depth discrimination requires the targeted statistical features our pipeline extracts rather than general language understanding.

Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1\% vs.\ 66.4\% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown decoding strategies infeasible.
A multi-temperature ablation ($\tau \in [0.5, 1.1]$, Pythia-1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:multi_tau}) reinforces this: within-$\tau$ depth discrimination is robust for $\tau \leq 0.9$ (d1v2 AUC $>0.80$), but cross-$\tau$ transfer (mean 46.7\%) is harder than cross-strategy transfer (59.1\%), confirming that strategy-conditioned classifiers are necessary.
A two-stage pipeline---first identifying the decoding strategy, then applying a strategy-conditioned depth classifier---could address this.
Different strategies produce distinguishable perplexity signatures (top-$k$ yields narrower distributions; temperature sampling produces heavier tails), suggesting that automatic strategy identification is technically feasible, though independent validation on held-out strategy sets is needed.
As an alternative, when deployment is restricted to a single platform or API provider, the decoding strategy is typically known a priori, and a strategy-conditioned classifier can be applied directly.

\paragraph{Depth-graduated data curation.}
Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction~\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
Depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) while filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
A proof-of-concept LoRA fine-tuning experiment shows RF depth-based filtering matches unfiltered performance with 44\% of the data, significantly outperforming size-matched random subsampling at all stringency tiers (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}).
Cross-strategy deployment would first require strategy identification to avoid boundary inversion (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}).

\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}
Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods---watermarking~\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} (requires generator cooperation) and source attribution~\cite{uchendu2020_attribution} (identifies model, not history)---by characterizing \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator identity~\cite{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms}.
A layered system combining watermark presence, source model, and recursive depth could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.

\paragraph{Mixed-depth documents.}
Sliding-window depth estimation at the segment level (256--512 tokens) could extend the approach to mixed-depth documents, enabling paragraph-level curation even from partially contaminated content.

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Perplexity tail statistics exhibit inherent resistance to surface-level transformations (paraphrasing, back-translation) that preserve surprisal structure, though robustness to targeted distribution-aware attacks remains unverified.

\paragraph{Scaling behavior.}
Our cross-scale experiments (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) confirm that depth signal persists at 7--8B scale (Llama-3.1-8B: 70.2\%, Qwen2.5-7B: 60.1\%).
Llama-3.1-8B matches the smaller models at $\mathrm{EDD}{=}4$ with monotonic AUC decay, while Qwen2.5-7B achieves $\mathrm{EDD}_{T{=}0.70} > 5$ via a non-monotonic (U-shaped) trajectory---exceeding the $\mathrm{EDD}{=}4$ at 1--1.5B.
Per-step signal strength decreases (mean consecutive AUC ${\approx}$0.78 vs.\ ${\approx}$0.85 at 1--1.5B), consistent with larger models generating more fluent text with narrower perplexity distributions.
The divergent AUC trajectories (monotonic for Llama-3.1 vs.\ U-shaped for Qwen2.5-Instruct) suggest that instruction tuning may alter degradation dynamics at high recursion depth, an observation warranting further investigation with controlled base/instruct pairs.
Tail erosion is driven by retraining on one's own output distribution rather than model capacity per se, explaining why the signal attenuates but does not vanish; further scaling beyond 8B may require richer feature sets (e.g., attention entropy or generation diversity metrics) to maintain discriminability.

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Problem Definition}
5	\label{sec:method:problem}
6	
7	Let $f_\theta$ denote a language model and $\mathcal{D}_0$ a corpus of human-written seed text.
8	We define a \emph{recursive generation chain} of depth $K$ as the sequence $\mathcal{D}_0, \mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_K$, where each $\mathcal{D}_k$ ($k \geq 1$) is produced by finetuning $f_\theta$ on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ and sampling from the resulting model.
9	Depth $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text; depth $d{=}k$ ($k \geq 1$) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-$(k{-}1)$ data.
10	
11	Given a text passage $x$, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth $d \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$.
12	This is an ordinal classification problem: depths carry a natural ordering, and $d{=}1$ is structurally closer to $d{=}0$ than $d{=}3$ is, since each generation step compounds distributional drift.
13	
14	\subsection{Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction}
15	\label{sec:method:benchmark}
16	
17	We construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.
18	
19	\paragraph{Model families.}
20	We select three 1--1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2~XL (OpenAI, 1.5B).
21	Restricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Decoding strategies.}
24	Each model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).
25	These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.
26	Our findings on feature importance and discriminability are limited to this grid; transfer to untested models, scales, or strategies is not established.
27	
28	\paragraph{Depth and scale.}
29	The primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total).
30	For depth extension experiments (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0--d5.
31	
32	\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}
33	Starting from a Wikipedia subset as seed text ($\mathcal{D}_0$), each generation cycle proceeds in three steps: (1)~LoRA finetuning \cite{hu2022lora} on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$, freezing base model weights and training low-rank update matrices ($<$1\% additional parameters; $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, 3 epochs, dropout $0.05$, architecture-specific targets); (2)~sampling 5{,}000 passages from the LoRA-finetuned model (max 512 tokens, BOS-seeded, no prompt conditioning) under the specified decoding strategy; (3)~the generated corpus becomes $\mathcal{D}_k$ for the next cycle.
34	Each depth is produced by a model explicitly trained on the prior depth's data---not by sampling from the unmodified base model.
35	There is no per-passage lineage across depths, ensuring cross-validation splits do not introduce information leakage.
36	
37	\paragraph{Reference model.}
38	All statistical features (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) are computed using a fixed reference model---Pythia-1.4B---providing a consistent perplexity reference across all generation conditions.
39	We select Pythia-1.4B because it is the smallest of the three generators, and its training corpus (The Pile) partially overlaps with those of OLMo and GPT-2~XL, keeping perplexity values in a comparable range.
40	For the Pythia pipeline, feature extraction constitutes self-model measurement; for OLMo and GPT-2~XL, it is cross-model.
41	Empirically, the Pythia pipeline's 4-class accuracy (78.2\%) does not exceed GPT-2~XL (85.4\%), indicating that self-model measurement does not confer a systematic advantage.
42	In cross-model leave-one-out evaluation (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), the reference model remains fixed regardless of which generator is held out; the implications of sharing the reference model with one generator are discussed in Limitations.
43	An ablation replacing Pythia-1.4B with OLMo-1B as reference model yields 74.5\% vs 78.5\%, suggesting that depth signal detection is not critically dependent on the specific reference model ($\Delta$=4.0pp, within the 5pp robustness threshold; Appendix~\ref{tab:ref_ablation}).
44	
45	\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}
46	\label{sec:method:features}
47	
48	We extract a feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ comprising 19 candidate features from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$; ablation (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) shows the top 5 achieve 97.6\% of full-set performance, and variance inflation analysis reveals VIF${>}$10 for 14--16 features, placing the effective independent dimensionality at ${\approx}$4--5.
49	The features fall into four categories (Table~\ref{tab:features}).
50	
51	\begin{table}[t]
52	\centering
53	\small
54	\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (Pythia-1.4B).}
55	\label{tab:features}
56	\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
57	\toprule
58	Category & Features & $n$ \\
59	\midrule
60	Perplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\
61	statistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\
62	\addlinespace
63	Surprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\
64	statistics & & \\
65	\addlinespace
66	Lexical & type--token ratio, hapax ratio, & 4 \\
67	diversity & bigram entropy, trigram entropy & \\
68	\addlinespace
69	Repetition & repeated 2/3/4-gram fractions & 3 \\
70	\bottomrule
71	\end{tabular}
72	\end{table}
73	
74	\emph{Perplexity statistics} (9 features) capture the per-token perplexity distribution via moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) and quantiles (p10--p90); tail quantiles prove especially informative as recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
75	\emph{Surprisal statistics} (3 features): mean, variance, and entropy of $-\log p(\text{token})$; surprisal variance captures second-order structure not redundant with perplexity moments.
76	\emph{Lexical diversity} (4 features): type--token ratio, hapax ratio, bigram/trigram entropy.
77	\emph{Repetition} (3 features): repeated $n$-gram fractions for $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$.
78	
79	\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
80	\label{sec:method:edd}
81	
82	Aggregate multi-class accuracy obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depth boundaries.
83	We introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) to formalize the frontier beyond which adjacent depths become statistically indistinguishable.
84	
85	\paragraph{Pairwise discriminability.}
86	Let $\mathcal{D} = \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$ denote the depth set and $T \in (0.5, 1.0]$ a discrimination threshold.
87	For each adjacent pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we define the pairwise discriminability $\mathrm{AUC}(d, d{+}1)$ as the area under the ROC curve of a dedicated binary Random Forest classifier (500 trees, $\lfloor\sqrt{19}\rfloor$ candidate features per split) trained on class-balanced data from $\mathbf{f}(x)$ (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) to distinguish depth-$d$ from depth-$(d{+}1)$ samples, evaluated via 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
88	Each pair uses an independent classifier, avoiding the decision boundary dilution that arises in multi-class settings (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}).
89	
90	\begin{definition}[Effective Discriminable Depth]
91	\label{def:edd}
92	The \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} at threshold $T$ is:
93	\begin{equation}
94	\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max \bigl\{ d^*{+}1 \,:\, \forall\, d' \leq d^*,\; \mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \geq T \bigr\}
95	\label{eq:edd}
96	\end{equation}
97	where $d^* \in \{0, \dots, K{-}1\}$. If\, $\mathrm{AUC}(0,1) < T$, then $\mathrm{EDD}_T = 0$.
98	\end{definition}
99	
100	$\mathrm{EDD}_T$ is the deepest depth $d$ such that every adjacent pair from $(0,1)$ through $(d{-}1, d)$ remains discriminable at level $T$.
101	The universal quantifier ensures EDD reports the longest \emph{contiguous} discriminable prefix rather than an isolated high-AUC pair at greater depth.\footnote{Our AUC profiles are empirically monotonically decreasing (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), so in practice $\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max\{d'{+}1 : \mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \geq T\}$. For non-monotonic profiles, the contiguous formulation is more conservative (see Limitations).}
102	We set $T{=}0.75$ as default; sensitivity at $T \in \{0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80\}$ is reported in \S\ref{sec:atlas}.
103	
104	\paragraph{Classifiers.}
105	Our primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, unconstrained depth, 5-fold stratified cross-validation).
106	We compare against CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral2020}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, a 2-layer cross-entropy MLP, logistic regression, and a single-feature baseline using mean perplexity alone; results appear in \S\ref{sec:generalization}.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:intro}
3	
4	The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
5	As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
6	This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.
7	
8	Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
9	Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
10	Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
11	The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
12	No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.
13	
14	Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{universal and scale-variant} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{universal and scale-variant} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.
Surprisingly, in one of two 7B models the AUC trajectory becomes non-monotonic, suggesting that instruction tuning may alter degradation dynamics rather than scale alone driving a qualitative shift.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
Given a text passage, we compute a feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---19 candidates capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity, though high multicollinearity concentrates the signal in ${\approx}$4--5 effective dimensions (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features})---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Task formalization and benchmark.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, introduce the EDD metric, and construct a 180K-sample benchmark spanning 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies $\times$ 4 depths.

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} A systematic $3 \times 3$ characterization reveals that \textsc{p90\_ppl} and \textsc{var\_surprisal} are universal depth markers (top-2 in 9/9 and 8/9 cells), decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories qualitatively, and depth discrimination persists through $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ recursive steps.

    \item \textbf{Generalization across seven axes (four in main text; three in appendix).} We demonstrate robustness beyond the training grid: cross-model recursive chains (84.75\%---depth signal accumulates across heterogeneous model boundaries), cross-scale to two 7B architectures (70.2\% and 60.1\%, with divergent AUC trajectories), cross-domain transfer to arXiv (74.1\%), temperature robustness ($\tau \in [0.5, 0.9]$), and reference model independence ($\Delta{=}4$\,pp). End-to-end transformers achieve only ${\sim}$59\% (19pp below feature-based), confirming that perplexity tail features encode signal inaccessible to standard PLM representations---while requiring only 19 features and a Random Forest for millisecond-scale, GPU-free inference.
\end{itemize}

319	\paragraph{Cross-model recursive chains.}

337	\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation.}
338	Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
339	Recursive generation depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) whose distributional properties remain close to the human source, while down-weighting or filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.

343	\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}

345	Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} provides high-confidence attribution when the generator cooperates but is inapplicable to unwatermarked text.
346	Source attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} identifies the generating model but not the generation history.
347	Depth estimation characterizes \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator cooperation or identity.
348	A layered provenance system combining these three signals---watermark presence, source model, and recursive generation depth---could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ across models; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
The dominant pair (\texttt{p90\_ppl} top-2 in 9/9 cells, \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 under SHAP) generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature} within this experimental scope.
Recent work corroborates this connection, identifying entropy decline as a measurable signal of recursive degradation that parallels the tail erosion our features capture~\cite{shi2025_closer_look}.
Zero-shot LLM baselines reinforce this view: DeepSeek V3.2 (36.2\%) and Qwen2.5-7B (30.4\%) exhibit complementary failure modes---the former predicts nearly all samples as d0 while the latter is biased toward d1---yet both perform near chance, confirming that depth discrimination requires the targeted statistical features our pipeline extracts rather than general language understanding.

Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1\% vs.\ 66.4\% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown decoding strategies infeasible.
A multi-temperature ablation ($\tau \in [0.5, 1.1]$, Pythia-1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:multi_tau}) reinforces this: within-$\tau$ depth discrimination is robust for $\tau \leq 0.9$ (d1v2 AUC $>0.80$), but cross-$\tau$ transfer (mean 46.7\%) is harder than cross-strategy transfer (59.1\%), confirming that strategy-conditioned classifiers are necessary.
A two-stage pipeline---first identifying the decoding strategy, then applying a strategy-conditioned depth classifier---could address this.
Different strategies produce distinguishable perplexity signatures (top-$k$ yields narrower distributions; temperature sampling produces heavier tails), suggesting that automatic strategy identification is technically feasible, though independent validation on held-out strategy sets is needed.
As an alternative, when deployment is restricted to a single platform or API provider, the decoding strategy is typically known a priori, and a strategy-conditioned classifier can be applied directly.

\paragraph{Depth-graduated data curation.}
Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction~\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
Depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) while filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
A proof-of-concept LoRA fine-tuning experiment shows RF depth-based filtering matches unfiltered performance with 44\% of the data, significantly outperforming size-matched random subsampling at all stringency tiers (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}).
Cross-strategy deployment would first require strategy identification to avoid boundary inversion (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}).

\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}
Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods---watermarking~\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} (requires generator cooperation) and source attribution~\cite{uchendu2020_attribution} (identifies model, not history)---by characterizing \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator identity~\cite{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms}.
A layered system combining watermark presence, source model, and recursive depth could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.

\paragraph{Mixed-depth documents.}
Sliding-window depth estimation at the segment level (256--512 tokens) could extend the approach to mixed-depth documents, enabling paragraph-level curation even from partially contaminated content.

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Perplexity tail statistics exhibit inherent resistance to surface-level transformations (paraphrasing, back-translation) that preserve surprisal structure, though robustness to targeted distribution-aware attacks remains unverified.

\paragraph{Scaling behavior.}
Our cross-scale experiments (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) confirm that depth signal persists at 7--8B scale (Llama-3.1-8B: 70.2\%, Qwen2.5-7B: 60.1\%).
Llama-3.1-8B matches the smaller models at $\mathrm{EDD}{=}4$ with monotonic AUC decay, while Qwen2.5-7B achieves $\mathrm{EDD}_{T{=}0.70} > 5$ via a non-monotonic (U-shaped) trajectory---exceeding the $\mathrm{EDD}{=}4$ at 1--1.5B.
Per-step signal strength decreases (mean consecutive AUC ${\approx}$0.78 vs.\ ${\approx}$0.85 at 1--1.5B), consistent with larger models generating more fluent text with narrower perplexity distributions.
The divergent AUC trajectories (monotonic for Llama-3.1 vs.\ U-shaped for Qwen2.5-Instruct) suggest that instruction tuning may alter degradation dynamics at high recursion depth, an observation warranting further investigation with controlled base/instruct pairs.
Tail erosion is driven by retraining on one's own output distribution rather than model capacity per se, explaining why the signal attenuates but does not vanish; further scaling beyond 8B may require richer feature sets (e.g., attention entropy or generation diversity metrics) to maintain discriminability.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{universal and scale-variant} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.
Surprisingly, in one of two 7B models the AUC trajectory becomes non-monotonic, suggesting that instruction tuning may alter degradation dynamics rather than scale alone driving a qualitative shift.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
Given a text passage, we compute a feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---19 candidates capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity, though high multicollinearity concentrates the signal in ${\approx}$4--5 effective dimensions (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features})---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Task formalization and benchmark.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, introduce the EDD metric, and construct a 180K-sample benchmark spanning 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies $\times$ 4 depths.

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} A systematic $3 \times 3$ characterization reveals that \textsc{p90\_ppl} and \textsc{var\_surprisal} are universal depth markers (top-2 in 9/9 and 8/9 cells), decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories qualitatively, and depth discrimination persists through $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ recursive steps.

    \item \textbf{Generalization across seven axes (four in main text; three in appendix).} We demonstrate robustness beyond the training grid: cross-model recursive chains (84.75\%---depth signal accumulates across heterogeneous model boundaries), cross-scale to two 7B architectures (70.2\% and 60.1\%, with divergent AUC trajectories), cross-domain transfer to arXiv (74.1\%), temperature robustness ($\tau \in [0.5, 0.9]$), and reference model independence ($\Delta{=}4$\,pp). End-to-end transformers achieve only ${\sim}$59\% (19pp below feature-based), confirming that perplexity tail features encode signal inaccessible to standard PLM representations---while requiring only 19 features and a Random Forest for millisecond-scale, GPU-free inference.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails, collapsing the output distribution.
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this via scaling laws distinguishing tail \emph{narrowing} from \emph{cutting}; \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} establish strong collapse guarantees, and \citet{dohmatob2024_demystified} analyze the regression case.
The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this to self-consuming models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff.
Mitigation strategies include retaining real data \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} and filtering via detection \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
Recent work identifies non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, fixed-point convergence \cite{marchi2024_heat_death}, contamination bounds \cite{wang2026_contamination}, curated pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
These works characterize degradation but assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
The detection literature, recently surveyed by \citet{wu2025_detection_survey}, spans statistical, model-based, and watermarking paradigms.
DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature as a zero-shot detection signal; Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024} improves efficiency via surrogate-model conditional curvature.
Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits perplexity ratios between related models, DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity, and GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} visualizes per-token likelihood ranks.
Fundamental limits exist: paraphrasing reduces detection to near chance \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase}, detection degrades under distribution shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and a generator barrier bounds performance when the generator is unknown \cite{pu2026_generator_barrier}.
Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster} trains classifiers on statistical features for binary detection, sharing our feature-engineering philosophy but not addressing depth; M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval} benchmarks multilingual detection, and DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt} uses divergent $n$-gram analysis.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} embeds detectable signals but requires proactive deployment.
All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains.
\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text rather than generation depth.
LOKI \cite{loki2025} benchmarks synthetic data detection across modalities but evaluates binary detection only.
\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, measuring forward degradation; our task performs the inverse, classifying depth from text alone.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses.
We adopt both as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) to confirm the signal is accessible to principled ordinal methods.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals: nucleus sampling maintains diversity \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, decoding parameters affect evaluation non-trivially \cite{finlayson2024_closing}, and strategy effects are model-dependent \cite{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded}.
\citet{wiher2022_decoding} systematically compare methods on surface-level properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} regulates output entropy via perplexity control.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects beyond single-pass text quality.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails, collapsing the output distribution.
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this via scaling laws distinguishing tail \emph{narrowing} from \emph{cutting}; \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} establish strong collapse guarantees, and \citet{dohmatob2024_demystified} analyze the regression case.
The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this to self-consuming models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff.
Mitigation strategies include retaining real data \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} and filtering via detection \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
Recent work identifies non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, fixed-point convergence \cite{marchi2024_heat_death}, contamination bounds \cite{wang2026_contamination}, curated pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
These works characterize degradation but assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
The detection literature, recently surveyed by \citet{wu2025_detection_survey}, spans statistical, model-based, and watermarking paradigms.
DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature as a zero-shot detection signal; Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024} improves efficiency via surrogate-model conditional curvature.
Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits perplexity ratios between related models, DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity, and GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} visualizes per-token likelihood ranks.
Fundamental limits exist: paraphrasing reduces detection to near chance \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase}, detection degrades under distribution shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and a generator barrier bounds performance when the generator is unknown \cite{pu2026_generator_barrier}.
Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster} trains classifiers on statistical features for binary detection, sharing our feature-engineering philosophy but not addressing depth; M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval} benchmarks multilingual detection, and DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt} uses divergent $n$-gram analysis.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} embeds detectable signals but requires proactive deployment.
All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains.
\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text rather than generation depth.
LOKI \cite{loki2025} benchmarks synthetic data detection across modalities but evaluates binary detection only.
\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, measuring forward quality degradation across iterative LLM rewrites.
Their framing is complementary but distinct: they characterize \emph{how} text degrades (measuring fluency, coherence, and factuality decay) without attempting to \emph{classify} which iteration a given passage comes from.
Our task performs the inverse---ordinal depth estimation from text alone---which requires discriminating between adjacent depths rather than merely detecting aggregate degradation trends.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses.
We adopt both as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) to confirm the signal is accessible to principled ordinal methods.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals: nucleus sampling maintains diversity \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, decoding parameters affect evaluation non-trivially \cite{finlayson2024_closing}, and strategy effects are model-dependent \cite{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded}.
\citet{wiher2022_decoding} systematically compare methods on surface-level properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} regulates output entropy via perplexity control.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects beyond single-pass text quality.

\begin{abstract}
As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
From each passage we extract a compact statistical fingerprint---19 candidate features dominated by perplexity tail statistics---computed against a fixed reference model.
A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%), with perplexity tail statistics emerging as consistent depth markers across all studied configurations.
Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for the best-characterized model family (Pythia, $p{=}0.001$; consistent direction across all three families with graded statistical support; \S4.4).
Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% (d1--d3 balanced accuracy: 55.4\%, $1.7\times$ chance); cross-model recursive chains---where each depth is generated by a different architecture---achieve 84.75\% accuracy, providing preliminary evidence consistent with a process-level depth signal.
Preliminary cross-scale observations on two 7B-scale generators yield 70.2\% accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}{=}4$) and 60.1\%, with divergent AUC trajectories possibly linked to instruction-tuning effects.
Applied to WikiText-103 and C4 web-crawl text, the classifiers maintain high d0 accuracy on editorial text while revealing model-dependent false positive rates on heterogeneous web content.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ across models; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
The dominant feature group---perplexity tail statistics (\texttt{p90\_ppl} top-2 in 9/9 cells, \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 under SHAP)---generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature} within this experimental scope.
Recent work corroborates this connection, identifying entropy decline as a measurable signal of recursive degradation that parallels the tail erosion our features capture~\cite{shi2025_closer_look}.
A surface-text ablation reinforces this view: zero-shot LLMs (DeepSeek V3.2 at 36.2\%, Qwen2.5-7B at 30.4\%) both perform near chance despite exhibiting complementary prediction biases, and the 42\,pp gap confirms that the depth signal resides in distributional statistics inaccessible from surface text alone (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}).

Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1\% vs.\ 66.4\% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown decoding strategies infeasible.
A multi-temperature ablation ($\tau \in [0.5, 1.1]$, Pythia-1.4B; Appendix~\ref{app:multi_tau}) reinforces this: within-$\tau$ depth discrimination is robust for $\tau \leq 0.9$ (d1v2 AUC $>0.80$), but cross-$\tau$ transfer (mean 46.7\%) is harder than cross-strategy transfer (59.1\%), confirming that strategy-conditioned classifiers are necessary.
A two-stage pipeline---first identifying the decoding strategy, then applying a strategy-conditioned depth classifier---could address this.
Different strategies produce distinguishable perplexity signatures (top-$k$ yields narrower distributions; temperature sampling produces heavier tails), suggesting that automatic strategy identification is technically feasible, though independent validation on held-out strategy sets is needed.
As an alternative, when deployment is restricted to a single platform or API provider, the decoding strategy is typically known a priori, and a strategy-conditioned classifier can be applied directly.

\paragraph{Depth-graduated data curation.}
Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction~\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
Depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) while filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
A pilot study (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}) yields an inconclusive comparison between RF-filtered and unfiltered conditions ($p>0.4$, $\mathrm{df}{=}4$), though RF-filtered subsets significantly outperform size-matched random subsampling ($p<0.001$--$0.02$); large-scale validation is needed to determine whether depth-based filtering provides a practical advantage over unfiltered training.
